overview: The Jurchen-led Jin dynasty ruled northern China from 1115 to 1234, after overthrowing the Liao. This is a different dynasty from the earlier Jin of late antiquity. The index dates of 1200 to 1279 are misleading: an existing map overlay represents 1115 to 1234, using a coarse outline to correct a base map that confines Jin mainly to the northeast.

periods.title: Rise and conquest
periods.summary: The Jurchen dynasty replaced Liao rule and extended its power into northern China.

periods.title: Northern Chinese empire
periods.summary: The conquest of Kaifeng drove the Song court south.

periods.title: The central capital
periods.summary: The court moved to the city now called Beijing in 1153.

periods.title: Retreat and final defeat
periods.summary: The court relocated to Kaifeng; the last rulers were defeated at Caizhou.

items.text: Wanyan Aguda founded the dynasty in 1115 in the region of modern Harbin. His successors moved their main court south: Beijing became the central capital in 1153, and Kaifeng became the refuge of the court in 1214. Those moves trace both expansion into northern China and the later pressure of Mongol invasion.

The conquest of 1127 displaced the Northern Song court, but diplomacy continued between the northern Jin and southern Song. A silk handscroll attributed to Yang Bangji may depict a Song delegation meeting its Jin hosts. Its exact subject is uncertain, yet its continued Northern Song painting style is part of the cultural story.

Jin government belonged to a longer history of institutions as well as conquest. Historian Tao Jing-shen examined how it inherited features of Northern Song government and passed institutions to later conquering dynasties. A change in the ruling house could alter who held power while retaining and reshaping ways of administering a large country.

Schooling could happen in Jurchen as well as Chinese. Emperor Shizong ordered translations of Chinese classics in 1164. A Song envoy traveling in 1169 or 1170 noticed a roadside sign in Baozhou advertising Jurchen studies. The detail makes the language visible beyond the palace: someone was offering lessons near an ordinary street.

The first Jurchen-language civil examinations were held in 1173. Candidates answered a policy question in at least500 characters. Preparing required translated books, teachers and practice in composition. This was an effort to build a literary culture in Jurchen, alongside examinations conducted in Chinese, rather than simply abandoning one language for another.

sections.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance

items.text: A tiger-shaped ceramic pillow in the University of Michigan collection was made during the Jin dynasty. It is a hard neck rest, a type that could keep carefully arranged hair above the bed. The tiger supplies the decoration rather than the softness. Henan and Shanxi kilns specialized in such Cizhou wares.

Another pillow, now in Montreal, carries a bird perched on bamboo and a maker's stamp naming the Zhang family. Its potters covered gray stoneware with white slip, painted in iron black and added a transparent glaze. A familiar household object can preserve both a workshop's name and the steps of its craft.

Luxury clothing could advertise a favorite elite activity. A surviving Jin silk brocade shows a falcon attacking a swan, woven with gilded strips against green silk. Historical descriptions connect this pattern with robes worn by Jurchen noblemen at the annual spring hunt. Fashion could tell a hunting story before its wearer said a word.

At Houma in Shanxi, the Jin tomb of Dong Ming contained a brick stage with five actor figures. Another Jin tomb at Ershui preserved written fragments of three story-singing pieces. Performance mattered enough to enter the imagined afterlife. These finds supply evidence for entertainment beyond the official histories of emperors and wars.

Money was more complicated than a dynasty inventing a banknote. Research on the period before the 1190s describes continued use of Northern Song copper coins and uneven supplies of cash. It interprets early Jin jiaochao as deposit certificates used to transfer funds. A paper claim on money and everyday cash did different jobs.

Medical learning produced arguments as well as remedies. The later History of Jin describes physician Liu Wansu writing several books and favoring medicines classified as cooling. He explained illness through the medical theories of his time. The biography preserves an influential approach to treatment, rather than evidence that every household used it.

sections.title: A painter's words and what survived

items.text: The late-twelfth-century painting Wind and Snow in the Fir Pines survives with the signature of Li Shan. It also accumulated inscriptions from later admirers, including a Qing emperor. A scroll can therefore have several historical layers: the Jin painting and its maker's signature belong to a different time from later collectors' comments.

The painter's original Chinese signature reads “平陽李山製”, translated by the Smithsonian as “Made by Li Shan of Pingyang.” It is a short, securely identified written sample from the Jin period. Chinese was one of the languages used in this Jurchen-ruled state; these characters are not a sample of the separate Jurchen script.

The Mongol conquest brought severe destruction between 1211 and 1234. Stone inscriptions studied by historian Jinping Wang also show how people rebuilt social relationships afterward in Shanxi. Buddhist monks, Daoist priests and women appear as participants in that changing society. The dynasty's defeat did not end the lives or history of its communities.

ending.text: Mongol and Southern Song forces defeated the last Jin court at Caizhou in 1234. This ended the dynasty, not the peoples of northern China or their cultural traditions. The index's 1279 cutoff belongs to the imported record and must not be treated as a second Jin fall.
